Subject: Burst mapping workbook: Redwood sizing intake

Kimberly / Ben,

Thanks again for the quick intro call this morning. As promised, attaching a short sample of our traffic so you can sketch a sizing for the Dedicated pool we discussed. High-level context: Axiom Edge runs an interactive developer-facing assistant (chat + code gen) and a batch reranking path. We're evaluating a reserved GPU commitment for predictable latency during weekday peak hours.

Quick numbers (top-of-mind):
- Daily active sessions (DAU): ~12k
- Typical concurrent active sessions (average): 220
- Peak concurrent (1-hour window): 1,500 (we see spikes during product launches)
- Prompt length (tokens): median 45, 90th pct 180
- Generated response length (tokens): median 80, 90th pct 420
- Ratio interactive:batch ~ 85:15
- Target p95 latency (generation only): <= 750ms for interactive flows

I've attached axiom_workload_sample.csv with a small token-by-request sample and the procurement contact (procurement@axiomedge.com) for contract discussion. Can you confirm what inputs you need to convert this into a first-pass GPU-seat/slot estimate (N x GPU type) and whether session affinity + prefix caching would materially change the sizing you propose?

Thanks,
Alex Dunn
Head of Platform
Axiom Edge

Attachments: axiom_workload_sample.csv (csv, ~120 rows)
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Dunn <alex@axiomedge.com>

Subject: Re: Burst mapping workbook: Redwood sizing intake

Alex — thanks for the sample and the context. This is a great start. A few clarifying items that let us turn this into a defensible first-pass seat estimate and an ops plan: 

Can you confirm / send the following (short answers work):
1) SLA and acceptable p99 (if any) for the interactive path — do you need hard p99s or a p95 guardrail?
2) Session length distribution: how many requests per session (median / p90)? Is state (KV cache) kept across requests?
3) Any long-running streaming responses vs single-shot generation (we saw some responses > 1k tokens in the sample) — are those common?
4) Expected dayparting: what % of traffic in peak hour vs off-peak?
5) Do you care about cost-first vs latency-first routing? We can advise smaller GPUs + aggressive batching versus larger GPUs pinned for low latency.
6) Any restrictions on model variants (quantized vs fp16) or on using shared caching / prefix pinning (security/PII concerns)?

Practical next step: if you can fill the redwood_preflight_form.pdf (two pages) and drop the completed CSV back, Ben and I will put together a 3-tier sizing: conservative (low-cost), balanced (recommended), and latency-first (SLA-backed). Also include any calendar windows you'd like for a 45-min technical deep-dive — Vivek will lead the runtime/ops portion.

I'll attach the preflight form here in case it helps.

—Kimberly
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood_preflight_form.pdf (fillable)
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Date: 2028-10-21T11:32:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Burst mapping workbook: Redwood sizing intake

Looping in notes from quick scan of Alex's CSV:
- Very bursty: 95th pct token length and response size skew heavy; batching efficacy will depend on whether those long responses are outliers or sustained.
- If they keep KV across session, prefix caching could save up to ~30-40% token work for repeated system prompts.
- For a first-pass, I suggest we model with: median prompt 45 / median response 80; 10% of requests are > 500 tokens responses.

I'll prototype a rough-seat calc assuming: 1) A100 80GB equiv, 2) concurrent effective tokens-per-second target to hit p95 750ms. We'll surface three configs for Kimberly to share.

Ben
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
From: Alex Dunn <alex@axiomedge.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>, procurement@axiomedge.com
Date: 2028-10-22T08:21:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Burst mapping workbook: Redwood sizing intake

Hi Kimberly / Ben — thanks for the checklist. Quick answers inline: 
1) SLA: we want p95 <= 750ms, p99 < 2.5s for interactive; p99 tightening could be a later add-on.
2) Session length: median 3 requests per session, p90 10. Yes, we keep lightweight KV state per session (user messages + short context) for 20 minutes.
3) Streaming: ~6% of requests are streaming (codegen, long-form explainers); those can be routed to larger GPUs or fall back.
4) Dayparting: 55% of daily traffic falls into two peak windows (11:00–14:00 and 18:00–20:00 local). Peak-hour spike multiplier historically x6 vs baseline.
5) Routing: latency-first for interactive, cost-first okay for batch rerank.
6) Model variants: we prefer fp16 or bfloat quantized recommended by Redwood; no constraints on quantization.

I've uploaded an expanded sample (attached) with session ids and token counts. Let us know if you want a wider export.

Alex
